e-481.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
e-481.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\sin {2\theta} =2\sin \theta \cos \theta\quad\Rightarrow\quad \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(2\theta) = \sin{\theta}\cos{\theta}.
$$

 

Letting $\theta= \dfrac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{1}{2} \sin \left(2\cdot \dfrac{x}{2} \right) &= \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2} \right)\cos\left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right)\[5pt]
\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x	&= \sin \left( \dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos  \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right).
  }
$$

 

Therefore, 

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \sin \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \cos \left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int \dfrac{1}{2}\sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \int \sin {x} \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2} \left( - \cos {x}\right )+C \[5pt]
								&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \cos {x}+C.	
	}
$$

e-484.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
e-484.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\cos^2\theta -\sin^2\theta=\cos 2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$ gives

$$
\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x = \cos 6x,
$$

and therefore,

$$
\eqalign{
		{\int} \left(\cos^2 3x - \sin^2 3x\right ) \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \cos 6x\, \textrm{d}x\
								&=\dfrac{1}{6}\sin6x+ C.\
                                                                
	}
$$

e-482.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Cosine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
e-482.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\cos^2{x}$ term, given by

$$
\cos{2x} =2\cos^2 x -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
\cos^2 x = \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right).
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\eqalign{
		\int \cos^2 x \, \textrm{d}x&=\int  \dfrac{1}{2} \left(\cos 2x +1 \right) \, \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
								&=\dfrac{1}{2}\int ( \cos {2x} +1) \textrm{d}x\[5pt]
                                                                 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\sin {2x} +x\right) + C\[5pt]
								&= \dfrac{1}{4}\sin {2x} +\dfrac{1}{2}x + C.
								
	}
$$

e-483.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
e-483.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the $\sin^2$ term: 

$$
\cos {2\theta}=1-2\sin^2\theta.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos {2\theta} \right )=\sin^2\theta.
$$

Letting $\theta = 3x$, we have

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\left(1-\cos {6x} \right )=\sin^2(3x).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sin}^{2}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: $\int (4-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x=$
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =4x-\frac{3}{2}(-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)+C \\  & =4x+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

a

b

4x−12cos⁡6x+C
d
−4−14cos⁡6x+C

4x+12cos⁡6x+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

sin⁡2θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ⇒12sin⁡(2θ)=sin⁡θcos⁡θ.

Letting θ=3x, we get 12sin⁡6x=sin⁡3xcos⁡3x.

Substituting this into our integral, we get

∫(4−3sin⁡3xcos⁡3x)dx=∫(4−3⋅12sin⁡6x)dx=4x−32(−16cos⁡6x)+C=4x+14cos⁡6x+C.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option b. Since sin(3x)cos(3x) = sin(6x)/2, integrating gives 4x + cos(6x)/4 + C. Differentiating this returns 4 − 3sin(3x)cos(3x).

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
content.problem: $\int (4-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x=$
content.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x & =\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (4-3\operatorname{sin}⁡3x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int (4-3\cdot \frac{1}{2}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =4x-\frac{3}{2}(-\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)+C \\  & =4x+\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14040629/assets/41304b7f8cbaf3df778e0f079a1651d2846f94dc74012db3b2ce936144eac8c7.png)

Find the area $A$ of the region in the $xy$-plane that is bounded by the curve $y=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}),$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{6}$ and $x=\frac{5\pi }{6},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
after.worked_solution:
The area of the region is given by

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x.
$$

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{2},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,{|}_{\pi /6}^{5\pi /6} \\  & =-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{5\pi }{6})+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =2\sqrt{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The area of the region is given by A=∫π/65π/64sin⁡(x2)cos⁡(x2)dx.

In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine: sin⁡2θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ

Letting θ=x2, we get sin⁡(x)=2sin⁡(x2)cos⁡(x2).

Substituting this into our integral, we get A=∫π/65π/64sin⁡(x2)cos⁡(x2)dx=∫π/65π/62sin⁡(x)dx=−2cos⁡(x)|π/65π/6=−2cos⁡(5π6)+2cos⁡(π6)=23.

decision.explanation: The double-angle identity gives sin(x/4)cos(x/4) = (1/2)sin(x/2). Its integral is (1/2)(−2cos(x/2)) + C = −cos(x/2) + C.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Calculate $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]+C \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Sine
content.problem: Calculate $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x.$
content.worked_solution:
In this case, we use the double-angle formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \,⇒\,\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\theta =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .
$$

 

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{x}{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})]+C \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

after.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
content.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{x}^{2}-{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int (3{x}^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3{x}^{2}+\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\text{d}x \\  & =3(\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C \\  & ={x}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

cos2⁡θ−sin2⁡θ=cos⁡2θ

Therefore,

∫(3cos2⁡x+1−3sin2⁡x)dx=∫[3(cos2⁡x−sin2⁡x)+1]dx=∫(3cos⁡2x+1)dx=3(12⋅sin⁡2x)+x+C=32sin⁡2x+x+C.

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Expressions Using the Double-Angle Formula for Cosine
content.worked_solution:
We can use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta 
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (3{cos}^{2}⁡x+1-3{sin}^{2}⁡x)\text{d}x & =\int [3({cos}^{2}⁡x-{sin}^{2}⁡x)+1]\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+1)\text{d}x \\  & =3(\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+x+C \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Submit

decision.explanation: The integrand simplifies to 2cos(6x) + 6x, with antiderivative sin(6x)/3 + 3x². The sine terms vanish at both bounds, leaving 3[(π/2)² − (π/6)²] = 2π²/3.

after.name: Question 9
after.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =3x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡6x={cos}^{2}⁡3x-{sin}^{2}⁡3x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}(2{cos}^{2}⁡3x-2{sin}^{2}⁡3x+6x)\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡6x+6x)\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{2}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+\frac{6}{2}{x}^{2})|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & ={(\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡6x+3{x}^{2})|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /2} \\  & =[\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )+3{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}]-[\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+3{(\frac{\pi }{6})}^{2}] \\  & =3(\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{36}) \\  & =\frac{2{\pi }^{2}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The double-angle identity gives cos²(4x) − sin²(4x) = cos(8x). Integrating yields (1/8)sin(8x) + C.

after.name: Question 10
after.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

Letting $\theta =4x,$ we get

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡8x={cos}^{2}⁡4x-{sin}^{2}⁡4x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({cos}^{2}⁡4x-{sin}^{2}⁡4x)\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡8x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡8x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since 2cos²(2x) = 1 + cos(4x), an antiderivative is x + sin(4x)/4 − x³/3. Evaluating from π to 2π gives π − 7π³/3 = π(3 − 7π²)/3.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Evaluate 
${\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =2x$, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡2x=2[\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi +2\pi -\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2{\pi }^{3}]-[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi +\pi -\frac{1}{3}{\pi }^{3}] \\  & =2\pi -\frac{8{\pi }^{3}}{3}-\pi +\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\pi -\frac{7{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\pi -7{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi (3-7{\pi }^{2})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

${\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x.$
content.worked_solution:
Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ term, given by

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =2{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -1.
$$

 

Rearranging, we have

$$
{cos}^{2}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta +1).
$$

Letting $\theta =2x$, we have

$$
2{cos}^{2}⁡2x=2[\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1)]=\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(2{cos}^{2}⁡2x-{x}^{2})\text{d}x & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+1-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4x+x-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3})|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi +2\pi -\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2{\pi }^{3}]-[\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡4\pi +\pi -\frac{1}{3}{\pi }^{3}] \\  & =2\pi -\frac{8{\pi }^{3}}{3}-\pi +\frac{{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\pi -\frac{7{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{3\pi -7{\pi }^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi (3-7{\pi }^{2})}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The curve is 1 + cos²(x) = 3/2 + cos(2x)/2 and is positive throughout. Its area is [3x/2 + sin(2x)/4] from −π/2 to π. The sine terms vanish, giving (3/2)(3π/2) = 9π/4.

The area of the region is given by A=∫−π/2π(2cos2⁡x+sin2⁡x)dx.

Here, we use the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the cos2⁡x term, given by

cos⁡2x=2cos2⁡x−1.

Rearranging, we have

cos2⁡x=12(cos⁡2x+1).

Hence, the area of the region is

A=∫−π/2π(cos2⁡x+1)dx=∫−π/2π[12(cos⁡2x+1)+1]dx=12∫−π/2π(cos⁡2x+3)dx=12(12sin⁡2x+3x)|−π/2π=12[(12sin⁡2π+3π)−(12sin⁡(−π)−3π2)]=12(3π+3π2)=12(9π2)=9π4.

decision.explanation: Using −2sin²(x) = cos(2x) − 1, the positive curve becomes y = 2x − 1 + cos(2x). The area is [x² − x + sin(2x)/2] from π/2 to π = 3π²/4 − π/2 = π(3π − 2)/4.

after.worked_solution:
The area of the region bounded by the curve $y=-2{sin}^{2}⁡x+2x,$ the $x$-axis and the lines $x=\frac{\pi }{2}$ and $x=\pi $ is 

$$
A={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-2{sin}^{2}⁡x+2x)\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1=-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(-2{sin}^{2}⁡x+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡2x-1+2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x-x+{x}^{2})|}_{\pi /2}^{\pi } \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi -\pi +{\pi }^{2}]-[\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{2})-\frac{\pi }{2}+\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{{2}^{2}}] \\  & =-\pi +{\pi }^{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}-\frac{{\pi }^{2}}{4} \\  & =\frac{4{\pi }^{2}-4\pi -{\pi }^{2}+2\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{3{\pi }^{2}-2\pi }{4} \\  & =\frac{\pi (3\pi -2)}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

The area of the region bounded by the curve y=−2sin2⁡x+2x, the x-axis and the lines x=π2 and x=π is A=∫π/2π(−2sin2⁡x+2x)dx.

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the sin2 term:

cos⁡2x=1−2sin2⁡x

We can rearrange the above formula as

cos⁡2x−1=−2sin2⁡x.

We can now integrate as follows:

A=∫π/2π(−2sin2⁡x+2x)dx=∫π/2π(cos⁡2x−1+2x)dx=(12sin⁡2x−x+x2)|π/2π=[12sin⁡2π−π+π2]−[12sin⁡(2⋅π2)−π2+π222]=−π+π2+π2−π24=4π2−4π−π2+2π4=3π2−2π4=π(3π−2)4

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the sin2 term:

cos⁡2x=1−2sin2⁡x

We can rearrange the above formula as

cos⁡2x−1=−2sin2⁡x.

We can now integrate as follows:

A=∫π/2π(−2sin2⁡x+2x)dx=∫π/2π(cos⁡2x−1+2x)dx=(12sin⁡2x−x+x2)|π/2π=[12sin⁡2π−π+π2]−[12sin⁡(2⋅π2)−π2+π222]=−π+π2+π2−π24=4π2−4π−π2+2π4=3π2−2π4=π(3π−2)4

decision.explanation: Using sin²(x) = (1 − cos(2x))/2, integrating term by term gives x/2 − sin(2x)/4 + C.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem: Calculate $\int {sin}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)={sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sin}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 17
?

Calculate ∫sin2⁡xdx.

a
x+12sin⁡2x+C
b
x+14sin⁡2x+C
c
x−14sin⁡2x+C
d
x2+12sin⁡2x+C
e
12x−14sin⁡2x+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the sin2 term:

cos⁡2x=1−2sin2⁡x. We can rearrange the above formula as

12(1−cos⁡2x)=sin2⁡x.

We can now integrate as follows:

∫sin2⁡xdx=∫12(1−cos⁡2x)dx=12∫(1−cos⁡2x)dx=12(x−12sin⁡2x)+C=12x−14sin⁡2x+C

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms option e. Since sin²(x) = (1 − cos(2x))/2, its integral is x/2 − sin(2x)/4 + C. Differentiating gives (1 − cos(2x))/2 = sin²(x).

content.knowledge_point: Integrating Using the Squared Sine Variant of the Cosine Double-Angle Formula
content.problem: Calculate $\int {sin}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$
content.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2x=1-2{sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)={sin}^{2}⁡x.
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {sin}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int (1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(x-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}x-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 18
after.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
\frac{1}{2}(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta )={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =\frac{x}{4},$ we have

$$
6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{4})=3(1-cos\,(\frac{x}{2})).
$$

We can now integrate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\,[6{sin}^{2}\,(\frac{x}{4})-3+3cos\,(\frac{x}{2})+x]dx & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,\,[3-3cos\,(\frac{x}{2})-3+3cos\,(\frac{x}{2})+x]dx \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }x\,dx \\  & ={\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}|}_{\pi }^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{(2\pi )^{2}-{\pi }^{2}}{2} \\  & =\frac{3{\pi }^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Calculate
$\int 6{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x.$
after.worked_solution:
Let's recall the double-angle formula for cosine that involves the ${sin}^{2}$ term: 

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta =1-2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta 
$$

We can rearrange the above formula as

$$
2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta =1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta .
$$

Letting $\theta =3x$, we have

$$
2{sin}^{2}⁡3x=1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x.
$$

Substituting this into our integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\cdot 2{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 3(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =3x-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡6x}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\int 6{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x & =\int 3\cdot 2{sin}^{2}⁡3x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int 3(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =\int (3-3\operatorname{cos}⁡6x)\text{d}x \\  & =3x-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡6x}{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$
